summary: First live exercise of myiotsan's actuation chokepoint, against a real device on the real embedded broker (tools/fleetbench/iotsan_harness.py + bench_iotsan_actuation.py). myiotsan is the app that WRITES to the physical world and it had never been run against anything - 11 test files, zero live exercise. Its whole safety story is one function, CommandService.Issue, and six ordered gates behind it: read-only by default, admin only, only-what-the-profile-declares, server-side bounds, a per-device duty cycle, and an audit row for every attempt INCLUDING every refusal. That is a claim about the whole program, and no unit test can check it - each caller's own test can pass while a caller nobody wrote a test for reaches the wire another way. So the bench enumerates every path that can move a device and drives each for real: the direct API, a scene, a schedule (test-fired AND fired by the clock), a flow's command node, a flow's mqtt_out node, and the rule engine. A paho client authenticated as the real provisioned device, confined by the real broker ACL, sits on that device's command topic throughout, so 'refused' means the API said no AND nothing arrived on the wire, and every negative assertion is conditioned on a positive that ran first on the same wire. It found one, and it is the one that mattered: the flow canvas's mqtt_out node publishes through broker.Publish - the server's OWN handle, subject to no ACL. Aimed at a device's command topic it moved a relay whose actuation was switched OFF, with a value outside the declared safe range, past the duty-cycle limit, and left nothing in the trail. Four gates bypassed at once, by the one node in the palette whose stated job is bridging a value out - and profile_command.go says outright that no such escape hatch exists, because one would be a remote shell for the building's electrics. A topic a real device would act on as a command is now RESERVED to the guarded path: refused when the flow is saved (naming the topic, the command and the device, and pointing at the command output instead) and refused again at run time, which is the authority and covers a flow drawn before this existed. The refused attempt is recorded in that device's command history like any other refusal, naming the flow as the actor. Any other topic still publishes - the bench checks that the bridge the node exists for still works. Everything else held up and is now proven rather than assumed: all six gates refuse for the right reason and nothing reaches the wire when they do; a refusal is still an audit row naming the actor; the bounds are a range, not a blanket no (the declared max is accepted and lands); an operator and a viewer are both refused actuation and can both still read the trail; scenes, schedules and flow command nodes all fan out through the same chokepoint and are refused with it; a schedule fired by the CLOCK is attributed to 'schedule:<name>' rather than reading 'System'; and the rule engine actuates nothing - rules alert. 45/45 against the fix, 41/45 against unfixed main.
compatibility: Backward-compatible for every intended use; no API, schema or configuration change. One behaviour deliberately changes: a flow's mqtt_out node can no longer publish to a topic that a device of this hub would act on as a command. Such a flow is refused when saved, with a message naming the topic and the device and pointing at the command output node; an existing flow that does it keeps saving and running but that one node now refuses instead of publishing, and writes the refusal into the device's command history. Any site relying on that to actuate was relying on a path that bypassed the actuation-enabled toggle, the declared bounds and the rate limit and recorded nothing - the command output node does the same job through the gates. Every other topic is unaffected, including a bridge topic that contains a device's own key. The reserved-topic set is cached for 30 seconds and invalidated whenever a profile is created, updated, imported or deleted.
